extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary criticism, poetry, and aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the evaluative principles and standards (Aristotelian and critical) for judging poetry and fine art: unity, imitation, plot construction, form vs matter, the aim of art, kinds of pleasure, and methods of representing the universal in the particular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on imitation / poetic truth
rubrics_metrics.description: He may recreate the actual, but he must avoid the lawless, the fantastic, the impossible. Poetic truth passes the bounds of reality, but it does not wantonly violate the laws which make the real world rational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry can transcend literal fact but must not 'wantonly violate' the rational laws of reality; avoid the lawless, the fantastic and impossible when aiming for poetic truth. This sets an anti-pattern: lawless/fantastic impossibilities undermine poetic credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic unity of the poetic work
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry ... acquires an ideal unity ... of the closer and more organic union of its parts. A whole is not a mere mass or sum of external parts which may be transposed at will; the parts which constitute it must be inwardly connected, arranged in a certain order, structurally related, and combined into a system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The work must behave like an organism: parts must cohere and be inwardly connected; removing or transposing parts should perceptibly affect the whole. Unity is an internal, structural property, not just thematic similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 'unity' and 'whole' (ordered structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: A unity is composed of a plurality of parts which cohere together and fall under a common idea, but are not necessarily combined in a definite order. The notion of a whole implies something more: the parts must be inwardly connected, arranged in a certain order, structurally related, and combined into a system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the piece merely groups related parts (unity) or actually orders them into a functioning whole; the latter is the stronger requirement for artistic success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of unity and plurality (size/proportion)
rubrics_metrics.description: By the rule, again, of beauty, which is a first requirement of art, a poetic creation must exhibit at once unity and plurality. If it is too small the whole is perceived but not the parts; if too large the parts are perceived but not the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge proportion and scale: a successful work shows both the integrity of the whole and the distinctness of parts; avoid works that are either too compressed or too diffuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot must be dramatically constructed (single action)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The plot must, as in a tragedy, be dramatically Constructed; it must have for its subject a single action, whole and complete, with a beginning, a Middle, and an end.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess narrative architecture: the plot should center on one coherent action and follow a clear beginning–middle–end progression. Fragmentary or multi-unfocused plots violate this Aristotelian criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form dominates matter; beauty as first requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: By the rule ... of beauty ... form dominates matter. The form or essence lives truly only in the mind of the artist who conceived the work; the matter passively receives the form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize structural/formal coherence and the 'idea' behind the work over mere material detail or external accoutrements. Evaluate how well form organizes and elevates chosen matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of the universal through the particular
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry ... approaches nearer to the universal. The aim of poetry is to represent the universal through the particular, to give a concrete and living embodiment of a universal truth. The universal of poetry is not an abstract idea; it is particularised to sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the specific scenes/characters/incidents illuminate broader truths without becoming abstract allegory; the universal should appear through vivid particularization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: general idea outlined then particularised from particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet is advised first to set forth his plot in its general idea ... abstracting the accidental features of time, place, and persons, and afterwards to fill it in with detail and incident and with proper names. He starts ... from a particular story ... He disentangles the main outline, adding or omitting as artistic purposes may require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate compositional method: begin with the main structural outline derived from particulars, abstract accidental features, then flesh out particulars; do not mistake this for imposing an abstract idea onto material (i.e., avoid pure allegory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confusing poetry with allegory (no literal embodiment of abstract idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Such a method does not imply that a general idea shall be embodied in a particular example—that is the method of allegory rather than that of poetry—but that the particular case shall be generalised by artistic treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag works that merely substitute a single abstract moral/idea for vivid character and situation as an anti-pattern; prefer works that generalise from rich particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters must be representative yet individualised
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry ... avoids and excludes all accident; its apparent individualities ... must be representative of a class, with generic attributes ... yet these class characteristics ... are so modified and particularised in each person ... that life itself does not excite more distinctly that sense of individuality which belongs to real existence. The individual form is uppermost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge characters for both 'representative' class traits (truthful probability given situation) and for particularising details that preserve individuality; generic attributes should be modified and personalised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstraction of accidentals (time/place/persons) as part of method
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstracting the accidental features of time, place, and persons, and afterwards to fill it in with detail ... The poet starts ... from a particular story ... He disentangles the main outline, adding or omitting as artistic purposes may require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether incidental contingencies are properly treated as accidental (and abstracted) so the work foregrounds essential causal/actional structure rather than flagging irrelevant details.

rubrics_metrics.name: End of fine art: pleasure (higher aesthetic pleasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of the fine arts is to produce pleasure. The pleasure, however, which is derived from an art may be of a higher or lower kind ... the higher Saywy7, artistic or philosophic, is the delight which comes from the ideal employment of leisure ... It is the pleasure peculiar to that state of rational enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the kind of pleasure produced: does the work create an elevated, reflective, or 'rational' pleasure (worthy of leisure and contemplation) rather than mere amusement or pastime?

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between serious art and pastime (moral/intellectual weight)
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful art ... may produce pleasure, but this is no part of its essence. Comedy is merely a form of sportive activity; the pleasure derived from it is of corresponding quality. Tragedy is the imitation of an action ... which is concerned with the supreme good or end of life; and the art which reproduces this aspect of life is itself a serious art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether a work aspires to serious, morally or philosophically significant representation (tragedy/serious art) versus light, recreational entertainment (pastime); seriousness correlates with higher aesthetic status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic enjoyment is primarily emotional (not purely intellectual)
rubrics_metrics.description: In his treatment of poetry ... he makes it plain that aesthetic enjoyment proper proceeds from an emotional rather than from an intellectual source. The main appeal is not to the reason but to the feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess emotional power and felt impact as central to success; intellectual cleverness alone is insufficient—emotional engagement is a primary criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art's end is for the spectator (audience-centered evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's theory has regard to the pleasure not of the maker, but of the ‘spectator’ who contemplates the finished product. The pleasure of art is not for the artist but for those who enjoy what he creates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the work's effectiveness in producing the intended effect on audiences/spectators; prioritize the work's reception and experiential impact over the artist's internal satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective end: realisation of a true idea (form realized in matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art as 'a faculty of production in accordance with a true idea' ... the object attains its end when the matter has been impressed with the artistic form (eidos), and the potential has been developed into the actual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how well the work realizes a coherent artistic idea in external form—the match between conceived form and chosen medium/matter is a measure of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection judged via subjective effect grounded in human nature; presence of a standard critic
rubrics_metrics.description: The work of art is in its nature to appeal to the senses and imagination of the person to whom it is presented; its perfection and success depend on a subjective impression. But the subjective emotion is deeply grounded in human nature ... a man of sound aesthetic instincts (a 'standard of taste') is assumed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both the subjective emotional effect on audiences and the existence of sound, trained aesthetic judgment as standard: not purely idiosyncratic taste but a cultivated, normative sensibility.
